transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-24 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 min
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Lucas Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (Acme Head of ML), Jonas Reuter (Acme Infra), Sara Lee (Acme Product)
Links shared: eval spreadsheet (drive link), security packet (redwood.link/soc2), benchmark plan (sheet link)

Summary:
Quick weekly check-in on POC quality eval. Reviewed latest scoring for prompt sets A/B/C, flagged 7 regressions (mostly hallucination/formatting), discussed guardrail tuning and acceptable thresholds, decided next steps for targeted regression runs and latency benchmark. Action items assigned.

Topics covered:
- Prompt set evaluation and scoring rubric
- Regression checks and diffing outputs
- Guardrails (toxic/bias filters, output schema enforcement)
- Latency vs cost tradeoffs (hosted vs dedicated)
- Security deliverables for pilot

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect):

[00:00] Maya Chen: Okay everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, we have Priya, Jonas, Sara from Acme, and Lucas and myself from Redwood. Is that right?

[00:06] Priya Patel: Yes, that is right. Hey Maya, hey Lucas.

[00:10] Jonas Reuter: Hey.

[00:12] Sara Lee: Hi all.

[00:18] Maya Chen: Cool. Agenda today — walk through the eval sheet, call out regressions since last week, talk about guardrails and thresholds, and set next steps. Lucas, are you good to kick off with the results?

[00:28] Lucas Ortiz: Yeah, sure. So we ran the 3 canonical prompt sets — Set A (customer support), Set B (summary/extraction), Set C (product recommendations) — against the pinned model variant we discussed, plus the fallback smaller quantized variant. I uploaded the sheet, there's a per-prompt score (0-5), and a pass/fail flag based on your criteria.

[00:45] Priya Patel: Quick note, our "pass" threshold is 4 or higher for critical prompts, right?

[00:50] Maya Chen: That's what we agreed last meeting, yes. We also have a soft pass of 3 for non-critical.

[00:55] Lucas Ortiz: Right. Overall, Set A average dropped from 4.2 to 3.8 — so we flagged 3 regressions there. Set B held steady at 4.0 but had formatting issues on two examples (extra punctuation, weird list ordering). Set C had two hallucination cases we marked as fail.

[01:20] Priya Patel: Can you open one of the hallucination examples? Which kinds of hallucinations — dates, invented facts, or product names?

[01:28] Lucas Ortiz: Mostly invented product specs and a wrongly inferred integration with a third-party tool. I'll read the example — prompt: "Integrate Acme with CloudDB for export" — expected answer: brief how-to + limitations; model output included a non-existent API endpoint "clouddb.exportAll()" which is wrong.

[01:45] Sara Lee: Ugh, yep that's risky for us. That would confuse our docs.

[01:48] Maya Chen: Understood. Two immediate levers: adjust guardrail to enforce schema and to strip code-like invents, and tune prompt to ask for 'do not invent functions or endpoints, if unsure say unknown'. We can add a high-precision classifier to catch code-like tokens.

[02:10] Priya Patel: How brittle is that? I mean if we add a classifier, does it add latency? We're sensitive to median< 200ms for support flow.

[02:18] Lucas Ortiz: Good point. Classifier approach can add ~20-50ms depending on host; if we run it as a light local check on the same GPU instance it's minimal. Alternatively, enforce via post-processing heuristics which are cheaper but less reliable for nuanced cases.

[02:35] Jonas Reuter: From infra side, we care about pipeline complexity. If we add post-processing services we may need additional containers and that affects cost. Curious to see numbers.

[02:44] Maya Chen: We'll include an estimated latency delta in the next spreadsheet push. Also note that dedicated capacity will shave per-token latency but costs more.

[02:52] Lucas Ortiz: On regressions diffs — I attached a diff tab where we show last good output vs current. For the 7 flagged cases, 4 are deterministic regressions (model changed behavior), 3 appear to be prompted-induced since we modified a prep template.

[03:05] Priya Patel: That prep template change came from our product edits last week — Sara, do you recall what changed?

[03:12] Sara Lee: We shortened the prompt to be more concise to reduce token count; maybe that removed the explicit "do not invent" line.

[03:18] Priya Patel: Okay that explains a couple. So action: we'll restore the explicit guardrail line for critical prompts.

[03:24] Maya Chen: Great. A couple more items we discussed — scoring rubric: we've marked false positives for toxicity as a separate column. Lucas, are we seeing any safety regressions?

[03:35] Lucas Ortiz: Nothing egregious; one case where the model used a phrase that could be borderline. We flagged it as 'needs review'. The safety classifier caught it but the threshold was low. We recommend tightening the filter for the product assistance flow.

[03:48] Priya Patel: What's the effort to tighten? Config change?

[03:51] Lucas Ortiz: It's a config change plus a quick PR if you want to keep version control — very low effort. Latency impact negligible.

[03:57] Jonas Reuter: On the VPC/private pilot question — we need the network diagram to get sign-off. Maya, you said you'd share that?

[04:04] Maya Chen: Yes, I'll send the SOC2 and network diagram after the call. Link will be in the next_steps.

[04:08] Priya Patel: Thanks.

[04:12] Lucas Ortiz: Another topic: regression testing cadence. We're proposing a nightly diff run for the critical 50 prompts and a weekly full sweep. Nightly diffs are lightweight and help catch model drift.

[04:22] Priya Patel: Nightly is good. Can the diffs produce actionable triage? Like a triage score that says model changed semantics vs formatting?

[04:30] Lucas Ortiz: Yes, we already tag diffs as 'semantic' or 'format' based on token-level heuristics and model embeddings distance. The tagging isn't perfect but it's high-precision for the common cases.

[04:45] Sara Lee: Embedding-based diffing sounds fancy. Is that extra cost?

[04:49] Lucas Ortiz: There's a small compute cost but it's minor compared to end-to-end serving. We can run diffs on CPU or on a low-cost instance.

[04:57] Maya Chen: Ok let's talk about thresholds. Priya mentioned critical is 4+. For nightly diffs we should set an alert if more than 5% of critical prompts regress or if any single critical prompt flips to fail. Thoughts?

[05:10] Priya Patel: Agree. Single critical failure should trigger a human review.

[05:13] Jonas Reuter: Also, flag if latency percentile shifts more than 10ms at p95. We don't want a silent scaling issue.

[05:20] Lucas Ortiz: Good call. We'll add p95 latency checks to the monitoring dashboard.

[05:24] Maya Chen: About model variants — we currently use the full float model as baseline and the quantized variant as fallback. Does the quantized one show worse hallucination rates?

[05:33] Lucas Ortiz: Slightly higher hallucination on a subset of knowledge-heavy prompts — about 2-3 more fails in Set C. That's expected with aggressive quantization. We can tune per-route routing so critical prompts always hit full variant.

[05:46] Priya Patel: That's fine as long as cost is manageable. We'll accept higher cost for critical flows.

[05:50] Sara Lee: Can we get a per-route cost estimate?

[05:53] Maya Chen: Yes, Lucas will add a per-route cost table to the sheet — tokens, compute, and expected monthly run-rate.

[06:00] Lucas Ortiz: I'll add that and also call out the difference between hosted and dedicated pricing. For dedicated, throughput is guaranteed but commit is required.

[06:08] Priya Patel: On benchmarking, we want a 10k token run that simulates peak concurrency to validate p95 numbers. Can Redwood run that in a dedicated slice for us?

[06:18] Maya Chen: We can run a dedicated benchmark during non-peak hours; we'll coordinate with Jonas for the peering window.

[06:24] Jonas Reuter: Window is typically 02:00-05:00 UTC, we can confirm.

[06:28] Priya Patel: Security note — we need an audit log of prompt inputs for a sample period. Is that possible in hosted?

[06:35] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood can provide audit logs for the pilot; for Private/Dedicated you'd have full control. We'll provide redacted examples in the security packet.

[06:44] Sara Lee: Also curious about RBAC — can we restrict who can deploy new prompt templates?

[06:48] Lucas Ortiz: Yes, RBAC exists in the console; we can show you the role mappings in the demo.

[06:53] Priya Patel: Great. One more question — any competitor notes? We compared to Anthropic's safety flow and an onprem vendor; the latter had better control but higher ops cost. Redwood's unified runtime is attractive.

[07:05] Maya Chen: Thanks. Quick recap and next steps?

[07:08] Maya Chen: Action items — Maya to share SOC2 and network diagram, Lucas to run targeted regression on 50 critical prompts, Maya to push updated eval sheet by Thursday, Acme to restore explicit guardrail lines on critical templates and share expected outputs. Schedule latency benchmark for next week window.

[07:25] Priya Patel: Sounds good.

[07:28] Jonas Reuter: I'll confirm the peering window and send firewall reqs.

[07:31] Sara Lee: We'll provide the expected outputs by Friday.

[07:34] Maya Chen: Perfect, thanks all. We'll follow up in email with links and assign in the sheet.

[07:40] (call ends)

Notes about transcription: occasional mis-attributions and filler words retained, some product names may be slightly mis-typed (e.g., "clouddb" vs Cloud DB).
